past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (stable, skin and joint involvement only)

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Normal language and cognition.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, right greater than left. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze — ptosis becomes complete on right side at 55 seconds. Diplopia on upgaze and rightward gaze. Mild right eye adduction weakness. Pupils equal and reactive. Mild dysarthria after sustained speech (>2 minutes). No facial sensory deficit. Palate symmetric at rest but slight nasal regurgitation of water on examination.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity: deltoids 4/5 bilaterally. Neck flexors: 3+/5. Distal strength preserved. Demonstrable fatigability — neck flexion strength drops from 3+ to 3-/5 after 30 seconds sustained effort.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal casual gait. Mild waddling pattern on prolonged walking.
neurological_exam.additional: No respiratory distress at rest. NIF -38 cmH2O. FVC 78% predicted. Neck weakness notable — patient cannot lift head off pillow against resistance.

patient.chief_complaint: Fluctuating ptosis, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing liquids
patient.history_present_illness: A 48-year-old woman with known SLE and Sjögren syndrome was referred to neurology after her rheumatologist noticed bilateral ptosis during a routine follow-up visit. She reports that she first noticed drooping of her right eyelid approximately 5 months ago, which she attributed to fatigue related to her lupus. She initially thought her Sjögren syndrome dry eyes were causing the eyelid heaviness. The ptosis became bilateral over 3 months and was accompanied by intermittent double vision, worse at the end of the day and on sustained lateral gaze. She mentions she has been having trouble swallowing liquids — she occasionally coughs when drinking water rapidly but can swallow solid foods without major difficulty. Her neck feels weak and she has been supporting her chin with her hand during prolonged reading. She initially discussed these symptoms with her rheumatologist, who increased her hydroxychloroquine dose thinking it was a lupus flare — this did not improve the neurological symptoms. She denies headache, sensory loss, or limb weakness at rest, though she notices she tires easily when blow-drying her hair (arm fatigue with overhead activities). She has not had any infections recently. She has a maternal aunt with myasthenia gravis, which her rheumatologist recalled and prompted the neurology referral. Her lupus has been otherwise stable — no joint flares, no rash worsening, no renal involvement. She is on hydroxychloroquine long-term and has had normal ophthalmology retinal checks.

specialized_test.impression: Borderline repetitive nerve stimulation results with 8-10% decremental responses. Nasalis exactly meets the 10% threshold. Given the clinical context (fatigable ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, neck weakness in a patient with a family history of MG and polyautoimmunity), these findings are consistent with myasthenia gravis. Single-fiber EMG is strongly recommended for higher sensitivity.
recommended_actions: Single-fiber EMG for definitive diagnosis given borderline RNS
Monitor respiratory function given neck weakness and dysphagia

In the setting of MG without thymoma, thymectomy is still beneficial (Class I evidence from MGTX trial) particularly for generalized MG in patients under 60.
recommended_actions: Thymoma excluded by CT — however, thymectomy referral still appropriate for generalized MG

results.title: Overlap syndromes in autoimmune neuromuscular disease
results.finding: MG-SLE overlap occurs in approximately 1-5% of MG patients; managing shared immunosuppression with mycophenolate or azathioprine is preferred; hydroxychloroquine is generally safe but rare reports of NMJ effects exist

results.title: Mycophenolate mofetil in myasthenia gravis
results.finding: MMF does not show steroid-sparing benefit in RCT, but observational data and clinical practice support its use as maintenance immunosuppression

results.title: MGTX trial — thymectomy in nonthymomatous MG
results.finding: Thymectomy + prednisone superior to prednisone alone in patients aged 18-65 with generalized MG; lower time-weighted average QMG score and fewer hospitalizations

output.summary: In MG-SLE overlap, mycophenolate mofetil is the preferred immunosuppressive agent as it benefits both conditions. Hydroxychloroquine is generally safe but rare NMJ effects reported. Thymectomy should be offered to patients under 65 with generalized AChR-positive MG regardless of CT findings per MGTX trial (2016).

abnormal_values_summary: All additional antibodies negative — AChR-MG confirmed

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, generalized, AChR antibody-positive (MGFA Class IIb), without thymoma, in setting of SLE/Sjögren overlap

differential.key_features: SLE can cause cranial nerve palsies but not fatigable pattern; anti-dsDNA mildly elevated but lupus cerebritis rare without other CNS signs; SFEMG would be normal
No baseline CMAP reduction; no >100% increment at 50Hz; no anti-VGCC; ocular symptoms prominent which is atypical for LEMS
CK normal; EMG shows NMJ pattern not inflammatory; no proximal limb pain; no skin rash (no overlap with dermatomyositis)
HCQ myopathy is rare, causes vacuolar myopathy with elevated CK; CK normal here; fatigable ocular symptoms not explained by HCQ myopathy

critical_actions: SFEMG is definitive — should not be deferred when serology and RNS are both borderline
Serial respiratory monitoring (NIF, FVC q4-6h) given borderline values and bulbar symptoms
Initiate IVIG or plasmapheresis if respiratory function worsens
Coordinate immunosuppression with rheumatology to avoid undertreating either SLE or MG
Thymectomy referral even without thymoma (MGTX trial supports benefit in generalized MG age <65)
Avoid hydroxychloroquine dose escalation during acute MG treatment phase
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT dismiss borderline serology as negative — AChR blocking and modulating antibodies confirm MG
Do NOT delay SFEMG when diagnosis uncertain — it has >95% sensitivity for generalized MG
Do NOT initiate high-dose steroids without hospitalization given borderline respiratory function (crisis risk)
Do NOT use fluoroquinolones (sulfa allergy noted; avoid fluoroquinolones separately as they worsen MG)
key_reasoning_points: Borderline AChR binding antibody alone is insufficient — abnormal blocking and modulating antibodies are independently diagnostic of AChR-MG
Polyautoimmunity (SLE + Sjögren + family history of MG) is a strong clinical predictor of MG diagnosis
SFEMG is the most sensitive test (>95%) and should be ordered whenever serology or RNS is borderline
CT chest shows no thymoma but thymectomy is still indicated per MGTX trial (Class I evidence) for generalized AChR-MG patients under 65
Mycophenolate mofetil is the preferred steroid-sparing agent in MG-SLE overlap as it benefits both conditions
Neck weakness with NIF -38 cmH2O represents moderate crisis risk — inpatient monitoring with serial pulmonary function is appropriate

red_herrings.data_point: Attributing ptosis and fatigue to SLE/Sjögren flare
red_herrings.intended_effect: Prior rheumatologist increased hydroxychloroquine thinking neurological symptoms were SLE — delay in MG diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: SLE does not cause fatigable ptosis and fatigable diplopia; NMJ dysfunction pattern is specific to MG; family history of MG and diurnal variation are strong MG clues
